Week 1: The Scene

Week 1 is the scene: the unit every piece of fiction is built from, and the five materials a scene is made of. The course takes one construction choice a week for twenty weeks. Each week you rewrite your own page every way that choice allows, then add new pages: a finished story by week 10, and a longer one by week 20.
The first ten weeks

The course climbs from the smallest unit of fiction to a whole story, one construction choice a week. Each week has the same four parts: the full set of options, one sentence-level joint, models to take apart, and pages due.

rows: scene and summary; five materials; eight kinds of scene
your page as a full scene
one moment in seven points of view
five ways to print a thought
six channels, five kinds, five engines
one supporting character built from a single line
five ways to print speech; the unsaid
a scene in which that line is spoken
a setting described in three orders

blocks.text: Weeks 11 to 20 have their own ladder at the top of Week 11: voice, irony, pattern, feeling, place, the strange, rhythm, the long form, cast, and your own style.
The method: same material, every way
Your own page is the material for all twenty weeks. Because the material stays fixed, every difference you feel between two versions belongs to the technique and to nothing else.
The patron of the method is Raymond Queneau. His Exercises in Style (1947) tells one small anecdote about a man on a Paris bus ninety-nine ways.
Choose one page to revisit all term. By week ten it should form part of a complete story; your alternative versions will record choices you decided against.
How a week runs
A week is six sessions of about an hour.

items: 1. Options. Read the week's tables, cover the first column, and name each option from its description.
2. Transposition. Rewrite a stretch of your page every way the week allows.
3. The joint. Do the sentence drill.
4. A master. Reverse-outline one model with the week's lens.
5. New pages. Write the pages due.
6. Aloud. Read the new pages out loud and mark every place you stumble.

blocks.text: The vocabulary kit runs beside this course. The kit supplies the words; this course supplies the places to put them.
What fiction is made of: five materials
Every sentence of fiction is one of five materials, and a writer's first skill is knowing which one is on the page. Cover the first column and name each from its signal.

rows: A page of nothing else reads as
what goes on inside a head
the teller compressing, explaining or judging

blocks.text: Your page, counted
Highlight each sentence with the color of its main material. Record the five totals. If thought and description dominate, underline where an external event alters what the character can do next.
A sustained interior monologue can move through associations instead of physical events. Track what pushes each thought into the next. Week 4 develops this technique.
Try replacing one stretch of reflection with a scene, then decide which version earns its place.
The scene, and every way to build one
A scene is one stretch of continuous time in one place, told at about the speed it happens. Everything else is summary: time compressed by a teller.
Neither is better. Summary covers years and sets terms; a scene puts the reader in the room. A story alternates the two, and choosing what gets a scene is the first act of construction.
"Show, don't tell" is half of this and misleading alone. Tolstoy and Austen tell on every page.
The five parts of a scene

rows: A school gym just before the auction closes.
what does someone want, right now?
The custodian wants a brass bell.
The bell has already been boxed for the successful bidder.
what is different by the end?
The bidder hears its cracked note and changes her mind.
The custodian carries the bell outside without ringing it.

blocks.text: Scene anatomy: place and hour → want → obstacle → turn → exit.
On a copy of your scene, fill in each box. An empty want or turn often explains why a vivid scene feels stationary.
A want can be small. Kurt Vonnegut's rule was that a character should want something, even if only a glass of water.
State a want in five words. Then write the first action somebody takes because of it.
Enter late and leave early: start after the scene has begun, and stop before it settles.
Eight kinds of scene
This is a working list. Most scenes in literature are one of these, or a cross of two.

rows: one person doing a thing, step by step
a stranger or a piece of news comes in
someone finds or learns a thing
O'Connor, "A Good Man Is Hard to Find"

blocks.text: The joint: the beat
A beat is the smallest unit of a scene: one thing happens, and something answers it. Scenes that feel static are usually missing the answers.
Write the answer in the order a body has it: sensation first, then movement, then words or thought. A reader trips when the order is reversed.
In each invented beat, the second event answers the first. Try three with different senses and verbs.

items: The rope slips. Mara catches its end against her shoe.
The bell rings once. Five bidders turn toward the empty platform.
A chalk number smears. The clerk reaches for his ledger.

blocks.text: Each line is a cause and an answer, and none of them is a thought. Thought comes back in once the beats can stand without it.
Three scenes to take apart
Compare three different mixtures of the five materials. Read each scene once for the experience and a second time to annotate it.

rows: speech and action; no reported thought
what each of the two wants; the subject they never name; where the scene enters and where it stops
which moments get a scene; how one paragraph covers months; what is different at the end
how one mark on a wall holds a whole monologue; what the last lines do to the rest

blocks.text: How to take a scene apart

items: 1. Number the paragraphs.
2. Label each with its material: A, S, T, D or Te.
3. Mark the want, the thing in the way, and the turn.
4. Measure the clock: how much time passes in the story, and in how many words.
5. Write one sentence: what would be lost if this were summary?

blocks.text: Drills and pages due
Do the drills in order; each one sets up the next.

items: 1. Count. Color your page by material and write down the five proportions.
2. Ten beats. Put a character in one place and write ten causes with ten answers. Use observable actions only.
3. Five leads. Rewrite the same moment five times, 150 words each. Let action, speech, thought, description and telling take turns leading.
4. Scene and summary. Compress one afternoon into a sentence, then expand one minute of it into 300 words.
5. Take apart the Hemingway with the five steps above.

blocks.text: Pages due: your page as a full scene, about 600 words. Give the narrator a want you can state in five words, put one thing in its way, and make one thing different at the end.
Sources
Checked: Exercises in Style for Queneau, and Iceberg theory for the unnamed subject of Hemingway's story.
The five materials, the five parts and the eight kinds of scene are this course's own working lists. Vonnegut's rule, the dates and the descriptions of the models are standard, given from memory.
Week 2: Point of View

Week 2 is the choice of teller: who speaks, how much they can know, how close they stand, and whether to believe them. You rewrite one moment of your page in seven points of view, then choose one for the story.
Every way to choose the teller

Point of view is four choices made at once: who speaks, what they can know, how close they stand, and whether we believe them. The nine standard combinations are below; cover the first column and name each.

rows: Who speaks, and what they can know
the main actor tells it, and knows only their own mind
Salinger, The Catcher in the Rye
a witness tells someone else's story
a "we" tells it: a town, a street, a class
the teller misreads or hides the story
Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day
a camera: only what could be seen and heard
several minds, one at a time
a teller who knows every mind, the past and the future

blocks.text: Retrospective and immediate narration cut across the nine choices. Compare “That sale taught me to listen” with “The bidding starts again.” A first-person narrator can also be reliable or unreliable; Wayne Booth developed the term unreliable narrator in 1961.
An immediate central narrator experiences a decision before its significance is known. A later narrator can supply hindsight, or knowingly withhold it.
Who sees and who speaks

Gérard Genette separates perception from narration: who sees and who speaks? An adult recalling a childhood quarrel can tell it in words unavailable to the child. With immediate narration, the two vantage points may coincide.
Hugh Kenner added a rule of thumb from Joyce, the Uncle Charles Principle: a narrator's words lean toward the idiom of the nearest character.
Five distances
John Gardner’s five distances move from an exterior view toward the character’s own language. Read the sequence aloud, then move the point of view outward again.

rows: Example: a mechanic at a lock gate
a place, an hour, a figure
On the canal bank, a worker stood beside a gate.
Mara had drawn the early shift.
her feeling, named by the teller
She dreaded lifting the latch herself.
her thought, in her own words
That rusted thing. It had to be today.

blocks.text: Distance moves like a camera: smoothly, and usually inward. A cut from step 1 to step 5 and back reads as a mistake.
One moment, seven points of view
Keep the event fixed: a mechanic tries to lift a jammed latch as a boat approaches. Compare what each teller can observe, remember or infer.

rows: I pull the latch. The boat is still coming.
I used to think the latch had jammed by accident.
We knew the morning shift by the sound of her wrench.
You pull until your gloves slide against the steel.
Mara pulled twice. A launch cut its motor.
Not stuck again. All those passengers watching her hand.
Mara blamed the rust. Below her, the lock keeper was still holding the pin.

blocks.text: The retrospective voice can correct an earlier belief. The group can gossip. In the objective account, a stopped motor conveys the stakes without naming an emotion.
The omniscient account can disclose a fact unavailable to the mechanic.
The joint: the filter verb

A filter verb reports the act of perceiving instead of the thing perceived: saw, heard, felt, noticed, watched, realized, wondered, seemed. In a close point of view everything on the page is already perceived, so the filter adds a step of distance.

rows: I saw the lock gate swing.
I felt the wrench slip in my hand.
She wondered who had moved the pin.

blocks.text: Keep the filter when noticing changes the event: “I noticed my fingers counting the links.” Cut it when it only repeats the point of view.
Read a filtered question aloud beside its bare equivalent. Keep the slower version if its hesitation matters to the voice.
Models to take apart
Each model isolates one of the week's choices. Read with a pencil and the task in the right-hand column.

rows: Mark each paragraph 1 to 5. Watch the teller start in a servant's idiom and end inside one man.
List what Nick sees, what he is told, and what he guesses.
Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day (1989), the first twenty pages
Find three places where the butler tells you less than you can see.
Ask who "we" is, what it knows, and when it learned it.

blocks.text: Drills and pages due
The first two drills are transpositions; the third is the joint.

items: 1. Seven tellers. Pick an event from your draft. Write it in each of the seven perspectives, about 100 words per version.
2. The ladder. Write one sentence of your page at each of the five distances.
3. Filter hunt. Circle every filter verb on your page. Cut them all, then restore the two that mattered.
4. Two selves. Add one sentence of hindsight to your page, from the narrator ten years on. Note what it does to the rest.
5. Track the distance through the first five pages of "The Dead".

blocks.text: Pages due: choose the point of view for your story and rewrite last week's 600 words in it. Add one paragraph that defends the choice by what this teller can and cannot know.
Sources
Checked: Uncle Charles Principle for Kenner, and Gérard Genette for focalization.
Further reading: Gardner, The Art of Fiction (1983); Booth, The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961). The practice ladder illustrates the movement through distance in new sentences.
Week 3: Time
Set the order, speed, frequency and tense of a narration. Tell one remembered event three ways, then give the story a clock.
Every way to handle time

A story makes four decisions about time: the order of telling, the speed, how often a thing is told, and the tense. Gérard Genette set out the first three in Narrative Discourse; the tables use plain names, with his in brackets.
Order

rows: cause, then effect; the reader learns as the character does
opens mid-action and fills in later
a past scene set inside the present one
the teller says what is coming
Spark, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
a present telling wraps an old story
scenes out of order, by association or design
Faulkner, The Sound and the Fury

blocks.text: Speed

rows: the story stops; the words go on

blocks.text: Five speeds, from quickest to slowest: gap, summary, scene, stretch, pause.
Compare the time that passes in the story to the words spent on it. A gap can skip years in a blank line. A pause can spend a paragraph while no story time passes.
Genette named four of these; later critics added the stretch.
A scene can sound like a pause when all the activity happens inside a character’s head. Insert one audible or visible change to let readers feel time passing.
Frequency

rows: Every Friday the ferry horn sounded at noon.
habit; a life in a sentence
Describe the same blast from the pier, the bridge and the waiting room.

blocks.text: Tense

rows: it cannot be held for long

blocks.text: One memory, three ways
A seamstress recalls missing a ferry. Keep the incident fixed and vary how much space the memory receives.

rows: the boat she missed that spring
Whenever a ticket tore, she saw the ferry cable lifting.
She ran onto the pier. The loose ticket stub slapped the boards. Above her, a deckhand folded the gate. Continue for a page in simple past.

blocks.text: In a present-tense frame, simple past can take the reader into memory. In a past-tense frame, establish the earlier time with past perfect, then switch to simple past.
One stretch and one summary

rows: The ticket hangs from the punch by a curl of green paper. A thumbnail catches the curl. For an instant the stub stands on its own.
She spent the crossing sorting tickets.

blocks.text: The joint: the bridge into the past
A flashback is three sentences of carpentry and then a scene. The three are a trigger, a tense shift and a return.

rows: a sensation in the present that the memory shares
the shift, in a present-tense story
one step into the simple past
The ferry gate clicked the same way that winter.
the shift, in a past-tense story
two or three "had"s, then the simple past
The ferry gate had jammed. She had pulled at it herself. Then a deckhand took the lever.
a present sensation, or a line of white space
The punch clicks again; a passenger holds out a ticket.

blocks.text: Smell and taste are the classic triggers. Proust hung seven volumes on a cake dipped in tea.
White space is the other bridge. A blank line can skip an hour or thirty years, and it asks nothing of the grammar. Use it when the jump is the point; use the three-part bridge when the link is.
Models to take apart
Each model pushes one of the week's dials to its limit.

rows: Find the sentence where the clock slows. Count the words spent on the instant after it, and note what the story lists before it reaches the one memory.
Woolf, Mrs Dalloway (1925), the first thirty pages
Mark every slide into the past. Write down the object or sound that carries each one, out and back.
Munro, "The Bear Came Over the Mountain" (1999)
Find the white space that jumps decades. Ask what the story gains by not showing those years.
Spark, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie (1961)
Note each time the teller says what will happen to a girl. Ask why the suspense survives.

items: 1. Tell one memory in a clause, in an iterative sentence and in a full 300-word scene.
2. Expand a single sound to 150 words. Compress the entire event into one sentence.
3. Frequency. Rewrite five sentences of your page as habits: "Every night..."
4. Tense. Put the first 200 words of your page in the past tense. List what you gained and what you lost.
5. Reverse. Outline the scene backward, from the last consequential detail to the first, in six lines.
6. Take apart "Bullet in the Brain" for speed: label each paragraph gap, summary, scene, stretch or pause.

Sources

Week 4: Consciousness
Represent a mind using third-person narration, an associative stream or a first-person monologue. Build and identify free indirect sentences.
Every way to print a thought

Fiction is the one art that can put a reader inside another mind, and there are five ways to do it. Dorrit Cohn named the three third-person modes in Transparent Minds (1978); the plain names here are mine, with hers in brackets.

rows: One thought about closing a shop
the teller's words and grammar; it can say what she does not know she feels
Leena was more afraid of giving up the key than she yet understood.
her exact words, present tense, tagged or in italics
“Where will I go tomorrow?” she thought.
her words in the teller's tense and person, no tag
Where would she go tomorrow, without the key?
thought before it is tidy: fragments, senses and memory mixed
Key. Cold edges. That squeak again, first morning, the little brass—
I turn it once more. One last time.

blocks.text: The narrator can describe an emotion its owner has yet to recognize. As diction approaches the character’s own words, knowledge narrows and the reader hears more of the character’s judgment.
The chain a mind runs
A page of thought moves by hand-offs. Each item passes to the next by likeness, by sound or by cause, and the reader follows as long as each hand-off can be felt.

rows: a key pressing into a palm
the sharp tooth of the key
the first day the shop opened
to turn the key once more

blocks.text: Mark every hand-off on your page and name its kind. Where you cannot name it, the reader falls off.
Self-correction

Catch a mind revising its own language. “I felt relieved. No: light. As if somebody else had lifted the counter.” Compare this with a settled account written years later. Beckett’s narrators repeatedly correct themselves this way.
The joint: free indirect style

Free indirect style gives a character's thought in the teller's tense and person, with no "she thought". It lets one sentence belong to two people at once, and it has been the novel's default interior since Austen and Flaubert.
The ladder

rows: She thought, “I will open late tomorrow.”
She thought that she would open late the next day.

blocks.text: Five markers

rows: the teller's tense and person stay
She could leave the shutters down.
the character's own vocabulary comes in
questions and exclamations stand with no tag
here-and-now words sit in a past-tense sentence
Tomorrow she had a new tenant.
She would hand over the key at noon.

blocks.text: A retrospective first person can also hold the younger self’s immediacy inside older grammar: “I had no shop tomorrow. What would I do at eight?”
The risk is doubt about who is judging. That doubt is also the point: irony lives in the gap between the teller's grammar and the character's words.
Models to take apart
The five models run from the most managed mind to the least.

rows: Austen, Emma (1815), the chapter after Mr. Elton's proposal
free indirect, early and already complete
Underline each sentence that is Emma's thought with no tag. Note where the teller steps back in.
free indirect that takes on a character's gush
Mark the exclamations and questions. Ask which of them the teller believes.
stream: short notes of thought inside third-person action
Bracket each fragment of Bloom's thought. Name the hand-off that brings it.
Woolf, "The Mark on the Wall" (1917), again
Number the returns to the mark. See how each return launches a longer flight.
Read three sections by three speakers. List the words only each one would use.

Use the drills to try modes different from the one you habitually use.

items: 1. Four modes. Take one paragraph of your page and write it in each of the four third-person modes.
2. The ladder. Take five thoughts from your page down the ladder: direct, indirect, free indirect.
3. The chain. Label every sentence of your page with its link. Circle each hand-off you cannot name.
4. Stream. Write 200 words with no full stop until the thought turns.

6. Take apart the Emma chapter with a pencil.

Week 5: Character
Build a character through six channels, five character types and five engines of action. Start with a single invented line of dialogue.
Every way to show a person
A character reaches the reader through six channels, and a strong one arrives through several at once. Cover the first column and name each.

rows: “If you wanted it, why did you stop?”
He withdraws his own bid to let a stranger win.
what she looks like and owns
The cuffs are frayed, the fountain pen spotless.
the inside, if the point of view allows
In his viewpoint, a bid can feel like a dare.
Another clerk calls him generous; a bidder calls him vain.
a flat statement: "She was a careful woman."
He had kept the ledger for fourteen years.

blocks.text: Try making an absent figure vivid through somebody else’s speech or memory, then consider what changes if the person appears in a scene.
Read a line closely
A clerk asks, “If you wanted it, why did you stop?” Read the two short clauses aloud. The second can put pressure on the person answering.
In one scene the question could be encouragement; in another it could be a public rebuke. Write the gesture that allows the reader to hear which one is intended.
Kinds of character

rows: built on one idea; summed up in a sentence
able to surprise in a convincing way
known only through others' talk and memory
set beside another to show them up
present to see, not to act

blocks.text: E. M. Forster drew the flat and round distinction in 1927. His test for a round character is whether she can surprise the reader and still convince.
What makes a person move

rows: what is she after in this scene?
what will she not look at?
which two true things about her fight?
what does she do without deciding to?
what does she know that the narrator does not?

blocks.text: The joint: the gesture

A gesture is one small physical act that only this person would do in just this way. One true gesture does more than a paragraph of adjectives, because the reader sees it and draws the conclusion alone.

rows: He squared a slip of paper with the ruled margin before writing the price.
A stock gesture and a label.
He capped the pen, uncapped it, and capped it again.
He wrote the winning bid through three sheets of carbon.

blocks.text: A gesture has three tests. Is it visible? Could another character do it the same way? Does it show something she would not say?
The best gestures are slightly wrong for the type. A thrifty woman who clips coupons is a label; a thrifty woman who overtips is a person.
Models to take apart
Each model builds a person by a different channel.

rows: a whole life in summary and detail
List ten objects in the story. Say what each tells you about Félicité that the teller never states.
Chart what Olenka believes under each attachment. Ask whether she changes or is only revealed.
Note every name and what it promises. Find the moment each person surprises you.
Welty, "Why I Live at the P.O." (1941)
Mark five sentences only Sister could say. Ask what she does not notice about herself.

blocks.text: Drills and pages due
All six drills build one person out of one sentence.

items: 1. Six channels. Write one supporting character through each channel in 60 words each.
2. Under the water. Answer twenty questions about her that will never reach the page: her first job, her shoes, what she fears at night.
3. Ten gestures. Write ten for her and keep one.
4. A flat character. Introduce a passerby in one sentence that entirely sums them up.
5. Give an animal or background character a want and an obstacle.
6. From outside. In 150 words, let the supporting figure observe the narrator.

blocks.text: Pages due: a 500-word scene from the past where your character first speaks the chosen line. Give the character a want and a distinctive gesture.
Sources
Checked: Aspects of the Novel for Forster's book and its date.
The six channels and five engines are working categories for this course. Check reading references against the editions you use.
Five ways to put speech on the page

A groundskeeper and a volunteer are deciding whether to open a greenhouse. Try this one exchange at five different distances. Give direct speech to the line that changes the scene. Other talk can move faster.

rows: Mara told Kit to leave the latch down.
The speaker’s words absorbed into the telling
Good heavens, did the latch have to come up this minute?
The fact and duration of talk
They spent half an hour arguing over the opening.
A summary gives way to one audible line
They argued until Mara said, “Those seedlings are the last ones.”

blocks.text: How speech is marked

rows: Make a boundary between speech and narration visible
Lets the voice sit closer to the telling
Tone, syntax and paragraphing carry the changes of voice

blocks.text: What is said, meant and unsaid

Write down the literal subject, the message a character hopes the other will hear, and what neither character dares to name. Hemingway’s iceberg comparison describes how knowledge omitted by the writer can still be felt. Read “Hills Like White Elephants” for an argument whose central issue is left implicit.

rows: “Is it open?” “The seedlings came through the frost.”
“Who kept the key?” “Have you had lunch?”
“We are extremely grateful for your supervision.”
Kit turned the visitors’ sign towards the wall.
Let the sound of the fan fill the space an answer should occupy.

blocks.text: The tag and the pause
A tag identifies the speaker. An action can identify the speaker and measure the pause before an answer. Read the first column without the explanations, then check which implications made it through.

rows: “Did anybody ask you to hold the keys?”
Kit held up a tray of empty pots. “Fine weather today.”

blocks.text: Identifying voices

Close the example with an action that answers an unspoken question. When Mara finally unhooks the spare key and leaves it by Kit’s elbow, the gesture gives up authority without naming it. Diction Week 9 supplies alternatives for the occasional moment that calls for a particular sound of voice.

rows: A conspicuous speech verb interprets the line. Spend such tags sparingly.
The first natural pause often identifies the speaker before the reader must guess.
An identifiable gesture can give the silence a duration.
Start a new paragraph for a new speaker
In a two-person exchange, distinct voices can carry the turns. Re-anchor after five or six lines if needed.

blocks.text: Reading the exchanges

First choose details, then order them, then decide whose mood selects and colors them. Figures of speech come later. Chekhov’s advice about conveying a moonlit night by the reflection in a shard of glass is a study in selection.

rows: Only the 8 on the clock face has lost its black paint.
A bunch of fresh herbs is tied to the luggage scale.

rows: Near to far or high to low
Give readers a place they can navigate.
Follow the character’s sequence of glances
Save the most disturbing or decisive object for last
Introduce objects as hands or feet encounter them
Keep action moving through the description.

blocks.text: Through whose mood

John Gardner’s barn exercise gives the observer a recent bereavement and asks the writer to communicate it without naming the loss. Try the same pair of objects seen by someone in two different states of mind. Eliot’s objective correlative gives a feeling a physical arrangement through which readers experience it.
Ten ways to make an image

rows: Give a thing its precise name
Compare while keeping both things visible
The signal arm dips like a conductor’s wrist.
Give one thing the identity of another
The barrier is a comb raking the crowd into lines.
The ticket machine refuses to reconsider.
Name something by an associated thing
Let a part stand for the whole
Six pairs of boots wait in the rain.
Borrow the vocabulary of one sense for another
A sour whistle carries across the tracks.
Show an ordinary object as a stranger might encounter it
A yellow arm slices the empty air into before and after.
The impatient wind keeps lifting the timetable.
Use a constellation of objects to carry the unnamed feeling
A folded ticket, two paper cups and one departing train.

The joint: the simile

Identify the subject, the thing compared to it, and the ground shared by both. A conductor’s wrist and a signal arm have the same brief downward movement. The comparison also changes how the departure feels: somebody has given the cue. Extend a simile across several clauses, as in Homer or Proust, or cut it short for comedy. Keep the original subject in view.

rows: Would this character plausibly know the thing used for comparison?
What emotion arrives with the resemblance?
Does each new clause earn the reader’s attention?
Is there one surprising, observable point of contact?

In chapter 1 of Flaubert’s Madame Bovary (1857), list the parts of the schoolboy’s cap in their order of appearance. Ask what their number and sequence suggest about the wearer.
Reading assignments

Further reading
Eliot on the objective correlative; Ruskin on pathetic fallacy; Shklovsky on defamiliarization; Gardner, The Art of Fiction; Chekhov’s advice in a letter to his brother.
Twelve ways to build a sentence

Hold one situation fixed while changing the grammar. In these examples a clockmaker restarts a town clock. Observe which constructions emphasize sequence, cause, qualification, accumulation or a delayed arrival.

rows: Coordinate clauses, often joined by and or but
The bell rings and the pigeons rise, but the square stays empty.
A main clause with ranked, dependent clauses
Because the wheel is cracked, the pointer jumps when it reaches twelve.
Main clause first, modifiers added after
Fenn held the wheel, fingers in the spokes, cheek against the casing.
After the oil, after the cleaning, after a winter’s patient filing, the clock struck.
Parallel halves turn on each other
The tower kept the town’s hours; the town kept the tower’s secrets.
A unit shorter than a clause

blocks.text: Five more constructions

rows: Omit and to clip the items
Repeat and to accumulate breath or ritual
The screw and the pin and the washer and the spring fell down the shaft.
An aside splits the main movement
The hand—if the brass stump deserved the name—pointed east.
A thought gets revised in the sentence
It was noon. No, it had once been noon.
Sustain grammatical continuity through several movements

The bell began with a rustle so small that Fenn took it for the shifting of the birds, and grew, as the hammer rose a second time and a third, until every cartwheel down in the square seemed to turn within that one sound.

blocks.text: Parataxis places clauses side by side. Hypotaxis subordinates one to another. Experiment with the difference between reporting that events follow and arguing that one event explains another.
Three registers

rows: Concrete, often short words; simple or coordinated clauses
Latinate or abstract vocabulary; long or periodic syntax

blocks.text: Cicero distinguishes these registers. Explore the vocabulary kit’s Latin families and sound families as two word stocks available to you.
The joint: cadence

The sentence ending determines where the ear comes to rest. Change only the last words and read three versions aloud. “The clock resumed its work at noon” puts the stress on a time. “At noon the silent clock struck” closes on a hard stressed verb. “The clock struck once and he listened to it” allows an unstressed pronoun to trail away.

items: Try ending on the word of greatest consequence.
Test a final stressed syllable for closure.
Try an unstressed ending when the thought should remain open.
Put a short sentence after a long one and hear the extra weight it acquires.
Read the passage aloud and mark the actual stresses.

blocks.text: Eight masters to copy by hand

Take a paragraph from a copy you can read. Write it out by hand slowly enough to notice how each clause joins the next, then apply the observed grammatical move to a paragraph of your own. Start with Hemingway’s opening of A Farewell to Arms (1929): count the repeated nouns and listen for how many relations “and” carries.

rows: A long sentence sustained through a boy’s sensory attention.
The postponed main clause and suspense created by qualification.
Rhythm built through repetition and intensification.
McCarthy, a landscape in Blood Meridian (1985)
Chains of “and”, old nouns and the absence of expected commas.
Lydia Davis, a story under one page
Ordinary vocabulary and unusually consequential word order.

blocks.text: Proust’s practice of pastiche offers a way to notice habits picked up from reading. Try an isolated grammatical feature deliberately, then decide whether it belongs in your prose.

items: Rewrite one sentence from your draft in all twelve constructions.

Write 150 words about changing light as one grammatical sentence.

Sources and checking

The constructions and three registers are tools from rhetoric. Consult the editions of the eight reading models you used and record passage or page references. Verify publication dates before citing them. For the deliberate imitation exercise, look at Proust’s pastiches.
Thirteen ways to shape a story
The arc is one possible route through material. Cover the names in the first column and identify each shape from its movement. This week you will outline the same work five ways, then choose a form.

rows: A want meets resistance, reaches crisis, and ends changed.
O’Connor, “A Good Man Is Hard to Find”
A small outer action ends in a change of perception.
The story stops as the central difficulty truly begins.
A final fact changes the meaning of earlier events.
A sequence of locations gives the story its steps.
One act of storytelling encloses another.
A bounded place or day contains a life.
Readers assemble meaning from separate pieces.
Gass, “In the Heart of the Heart of the Country”
An inventory or other practical form carries the story.
The same premises appear again under different conditions.

blocks.text: Two further shapes

rows: A stripped-down action supports meanings beyond the literal.
The end turns into the beginning.

blocks.text: Draw eight shapes

rows: Draw a line rising from want to crisis, then falling to a changed situation.
Draw a level line and mark a change of sight at its far end.
Turn the line back sharply at the final revelation.
Connect a series of places in order.
Draw the inner story inside the outer act of telling.
Alternate strands and mark the point at which they meet.
Arrange separate pieces with gaps the reader must cross.
Bring the last point back to the first.

blocks.text: The source diagram represents these eight forms; open ending, vigil, list, variations and parable depend more on the manner of telling. Aristotle’s beginning, middle and end permits many shapes. Freytag’s 1863 pyramid was built for five-act drama: introduction, rise, climax, fall and catastrophe.
Story and plot
Forster tests story with “and then” and plot with “because”. A sequence can loosen the causal chain, but consider what invitation carries the reader to the next page.
Four engines of tension

rows: When will the character discover it?
The reader knows more than the character.
What is this adding up to?
A repetition that changes with each return

blocks.text: A nearly motionless scene can run on pattern. Let the same fault appear in three different official forms. A reader may turn the page to discover the connection before anyone confronts it.
The joint: the turn and the white space

rows: Where one item violates the pattern

blocks.text: Locate the point where preparation becomes consequence. A blank line can change time, place, perspective or subject. Set two sections side by side, remove the explanation between them, and ask what the reader can infer.
One set of pieces in five forms
Use one invented situation throughout: a portrait goes missing from a market hall, a restorer has a duplicate frame, a clerk records deliveries, and a stamp appears twice in a ledger.

rows: The restorer must find the portrait before the exhibition opens. The repeated stamp reveals that it was delivered to the wrong hall.
The clerk gradually realizes the deliveries were accurate: there were two portraits, each believed to be unique.
Alternate hanging the show, making the frame, and filling the ledger. The stamp appears in all three strands.
An inventory of wall fittings, receipts and frames ends with one item no institution has a category for.
Begin with the recovered portrait; move back through the discovery to the clerk innocently stamping the first receipt.

rows: Find the last external event. Examine how what follows changes its meaning.
Reread with the final fact in mind. Mark earlier lines that now mean something else.

Assemble a finished story of about 3,000 words. Try an opening, an ending and a title together before choosing. Each first page makes promises that shape what the reader expects the ending to do.
Seven openings

rows: In the middle of a scene
Mara eased the plaster number off the wall.
Any building can keep a secret until its owner sells it.
A building number lay face down in the drain like a playing card.
“You’ll have to collect it before they change the locks.”
A teller who sees the whole duration
For six winters we went on sorting letters to a street that had vanished.
The reader will ask how this came about.
By closing time a hundred unclaimed keys would lie on the steps.
A matter-of-fact relation to the story
The auctioneer listed the building for one coin.

blocks.text: Eight endings

rows: A want is met or lost for good.
O’Connor, “A Good Man Is Hard to Find”
The story stops where the deeper difficulty begins.
A final picture carries the feeling.
A final fact reinterprets the rest.
An opening image returns under changed conditions.
The teller steps back and surveys a larger span.
Action stops before the response arrives.

blocks.text: Try a last image that leaves a question open. If a locksmith posts a single key through a sealed letterbox, the final object can carry several earlier decisions without resolving them aloud.

rows: Try it on the invented story

A six-movement plan is a starting point for an arc or a braid. Move the pieces according to your chosen shape. In this arrangement a two-person encounter gets the most space and the setting is distributed through the other sections.

rows: Establish the voice, a want, and the first obstacle.
Build a complete past scene with a bridge in and out.
A deeper return to the present
Let the mind move through a chain of thoughts.
A spoken line turns the encounter.
Put objects, surfaces and distances where they do something.
Bring back a changed detail and deliver the chosen turn.

blocks.text: The joint: first and last sentences

The first line fixes person, tense, distance and register, and opens a question. Read the last line immediately after it. For the building story, try “We keep every key.” Then try “This one we left in the door.” Keeping the person and plain register makes the change in that rule audible. Test another pairing in which the ending leaves the initial question open.
Five revision passes
Revise from large decisions down to the word. Moving or cutting a scene comes before polishing its sentences.

rows: Does the turn divide the story in the right place?
Does each scene contain a want, resistance and change?
Does the viewpoint hold, and can readers follow every temporal jump?
Is each material doing its job? Is description placed throughout?
Do the endings carry stress and do the nouns name exact things?

items: State the narrator’s want in five words.

Find the bridge or deliberate section break at every jump in time.
Remove dialogue tags and check that the speakers remain distinguishable.
Leave the most important issue unspoken. Can a reader still find it?
Find a detail on each page particular to this observer.
Read aloud and flag any sentence that takes your breath away by accident.

rows: A second strand and a substantial jump in time become possible.
Alice Munro, “The Bear Came Over the Mountain”

Kafka, The Metamorphosis; Claire Keegan, Small Things Like These
Separate stories share people or a place.
Joyce, Dubliners; Elizabeth Strout, Olive Kitteridge
Chapters, subplots, a schedule of tellers and a clock that may run for years.

rows: Plausible events made particular in their execution.
One impossible premise is treated as fact.
The marvelous arrives in a level narrative voice.
A house or landscape seems to hold concealed knowledge.
A distortion exposes a recognizable social order.

The teller and author share a public name or identity.

The six components of voice

rows: Try it on one witness at an observatory open night
The volunteer calls a galaxy a smudge.
A long instruction followed by a single-word afterthought.
How does the teller regard the event?
Mild amusement that everyone brought umbrellas on a clear night.
An absent colleague who needs the keys tomorrow.
The speaker revises precise times into round numbers.
A loose lens cap, a short queue, the smell of damp coats.

blocks.text: Ten tones, part one
Cover the names in the first column and identify each attitude. Try the same exercise with sentences from your own story.

rows: The literal words leave room for a different judgment
Treats an odd event as routine

blocks.text: Ten tones, continued

rows: Dwells on sound, image and cadence
Enjoys the distance between behavior and the words used for it
Speaks with an awareness of loss
Records what can be observed with a cool precision
Admits the listener to a secret
Speaks with the authority of a pronouncement
Returns to an idea as if unable to stop

blocks.text: Skaz is narration shaped by a speaking voice. A narrator’s dialect, slang or private turns of phrase govern the telling outside dialogue, too. Look for the technique in Gogol and Leskov.
A writer’s card: Nabokov

rows: An articulate, charming first person gives readers reason to doubt the account.
The reader may be treated as spectator or juror.
Exact sound and long syntax allow an aside inside another remark.
Precise unusual words, puns and significant names repay attention.
Doubles, dates and colors recur in patterns.
A frame can hold a document, confession or commentary.
An aside and one unexpected adjective whose meaning is exact.

blocks.text: A voice turns aside

Example: “We issued the guests a map (the building has two rooms) and bade them consult it at every turn.” The events could fit in a report. The parenthesis tells us what the speaker thinks of the organizers.

rows: Slips in a quiet second thought
The director (an excellent queue of one) waited by the door.
Three people cheered—four, if the echo counts.
You hear the mind revise itself
It was silent. Hushed, I mean.
Invites the reader into the telling
You can guess who had the spare pen.
Opens a doubt about what was just said
We opened on time. By whose clock?

rows: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, chapter 1
A boy’s speaking voice shapes the narration.
List ten departures from schoolroom grammar. Record what Huck sees that an adult might pass over.

An entire marriage compressed into plain talk
Count the comic sentences. Find one sentence that changes the tone.

Follow one repeated phrase for ten pages. Record what its returns add.

Four places to put the gap
Irony depends on a difference between what words seem to say and what events reveal. Hide the first column and identify which sort of difference each example uses.

rows: “Perfect timing,” says the conductor as the last passenger misses the departure.
The reader knows something the character has yet to learn.
The audience has seen the spare ticket inside the envelope the traveler discards.
An action produces the opposite of its intended result.
The clerk installs an express desk; everyone joins it and the ordinary desk stands empty.
A narrator persistently misreads the events being told.
Consider the butler’s interpretation of service in The Remains of the Day.

blocks.text: Five unreliable tellers, part one
Wayne Booth’s term “unreliable narrator” helps describe a difference between a teller’s interpretation and the judgment the book invites. Identify what makes an account difficult to trust.

rows: Cannot bear what an honest reading would imply
Kazuo Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day
Reports accurately but lacks the experience to interpret the facts

blocks.text: Five unreliable tellers, continued

rows: Lacks access to the event or the information
Ford Madox Ford, The Good Soldier

blocks.text: A clerk explains a silent room by blaming a faulty bell. The reader has just seen a notice cancelling the meeting. Sustaining the clerk’s explanation creates structural irony. Grant the clerk a convincing reason for holding it. Sympathy keeps perceptiveness from turning into a sneer.
A writer’s card: Chekhov

rows: Even third person leaves verdicts to the reader.
Come close for a paragraph, then step back.
Alternate scene with summary; one sentence can carry years.
Show what someone does immediately after making a fine declaration.
Two or three exact things can establish a whole setting.
The story can stop where the central difficulty begins.
Place a small plain fact beside a large feeling.

blocks.text: Example: “There were thirty chairs. He had borrowed ten more from the school. At quarter past seven he began putting those ten away.”
The joint: understatement
In the chair example, the extra ten chairs reveal how many people the organizer expected. Stay with an action the reader can see. As the event grows larger, try a smaller sentence.

rows: It was not our best opening.
Give one plain fact and stop
She was inconsolable when the club dissolved.
She put its key beside her plate.

Ford, The Good Soldier, part one

Retell the event in about 800 words. The teller should stay mistaken about a motive or cause, while the reader can identify the real one by the final line.

How meaning gathers through repetition

Let an ordinary object appear before it carries an obvious meaning. When it returns, its context changes what the reader sees. Try three appearances: introduce it, bring it back, then change something about the final appearance.

rows: An image, phrase or detail recurs
An object gathers an unstated significance
The green light in The Great Gatsby
A recurring phrase or detail signals a particular person
Something introduced early later matters to the action
An exit ticket shown at breakfast matters at the station
A later scene repeats the arrangement of an earlier one with a difference
A small sign gains significance through a later event
A cough early in a nineteenth-century novel
A name directs attention toward a pattern
The question the recurring details keep raising
What would it take for these neighbors to trust one another?

blocks.text: Inventory what is already in the story before putting in a symbol. A good prospect is an object a character has practical reasons to handle more than once.
Find the pattern in a draft

A rehearsal leader straightens a music stand, a row of chairs and a program on the lectern. Later she cannot bring herself to straighten an empty chair. The ordinary gesture acquires a meaning the narrator never has to state. Turn that meaning into a question to leave the reader room to answer.
A writer’s card: Joyce

rows: Third person moves into the words and attitudes of the person nearby.
Name a few everyday objects plainly and return to them.
Let cadence give emotional weight to simple words.
The action may be small while recognition grows on the last page.
Supplies a key to the pattern.
Give an image enough time on the page to hold.
Introduce one object three times. Enlarge its significance a little each time.

blocks.text: Example: “The brass counter clicked for each visitor. When it clicked again he was alone. He could remember years of standing at this door, his thumb going down.” The final sentence enlarges an ordinary action into a working life.
The joint: the echo

Begin with a detail that has a straightforward purpose. At its return, change a word, shorten the phrase or move it into a new context. Aim for a connection the reader feels before consciously tracing it. Vocabulary Week 7 offers the related idea of a refrain.

rows: One substituted noun changes who belongs.
The map ended at the gate.
Every route ended at the gate.
A property of one map becomes a feature of the whole place.
The shorter return can now refer to a person.

To let a reader experience an emotion, choose evidence a reader can interpret. Naming the emotion can also be effective once preceding details have earned the name. Try the six methods on a guest who worries that a promised speaker will fail to appear.
