rows: Reduce the reaction with the understatement exercise from Week 12.
Readers lack a way to enter the experience.
Supply one sensation in one particular place.
The same tears, pounding pulse or clenched hands would fit almost anyone.
Give this particular character a revealing gesture.

blocks.text: Chekhov’s advice about a cool manner is worth trying on a scene that asks for pity. An ordinary action can carry a strong emotion when the tone allows the reader to discover it.
The vocabulary of discomfort

In “On Being Ill,” Virginia Woolf draws attention to how few words ordinary language offers for bodily discomfort. Try a fictional traveler who has held a stiff arm still for too long. Can the reader locate the sensation without a general discomfort word?
A writer’s card: Tolstoy

rows: A calm omniscient narrator can see what a character cannot admit.
Follow one feeling as it changes into another in real time.
Find one involuntary movement, such as a change of gait.
Repeat a plain word when it remains the right one.
Describe a familiar object as if the viewer had just discovered it.

blocks.text: Mind and body can tell different stories

rows: Allow room for thought in a long sentence, then give the observable fact in a short one.
Place a person’s explanation beside what that person’s body does.

blocks.text: Example: “He had stepped aside, he decided, to let the ushers work. From behind the curtain his hand reached out twice to straighten the speaker’s card.” What he tells himself and what his hand does give the reader different accounts.
The joint: one bodily location, one verb
Choose one precise place and give it one verb. Try the line without an adverb. Vocabulary Week 19 has terms for parts of the body that rarely appear in a stock gesture.

rows: The tip of her tongue rested against a chipped tooth.
His forearms sagged against the desk.
The soles of her feet slid inside her shoes.
A muscle jumped beside his nostril.
A thread pulled from the crook of her elbow to her wrist.

blocks.text: Model readings

rows: Tolstoy, The Death of Ivan Ilyich
Physical illness and resistance to recognizing it
Mark each place where discomfort is located in the body. Track how long death can go unnamed.
Grief in search of a listener
List the people the cabman tries to tell. Whom can he finally address?
Find the named feelings. Consider the bread at the end.
Emotion carried in the account of music
Underline bodily language in the closing pages. Who is watching whom?

blocks.text: Drills

items: 1. Write 300 words about a fictional bodily discomfort without using pain, hurt, ache, sore or throb.
2. Give five feelings one sentence each, with a single bodily location and verb.
3. Look for tears, sighs, clenched fists and racing hearts in your draft. Replace three stock gestures.
4. Mark each named feeling. Remove the name temporarily and test what the rest of the scene conveys.
5. Show one character’s dread of a coming event with each of the six methods.
6. Write 150 words in which the teller recognizes a feeling that the character misidentifies. Use the Tolstoy card to guide the distance.

blocks.text: Pages due

Rewrite a scene of roughly 500 words around a physical sensation without using a word for pain. Then write a second scene that names a feeling once, choosing the moment when that single word carries the greatest weight.
Source notes
The course draws on a letter of Chekhov’s about writing with restraint and Woolf’s essay “On Being Ill.” The Tolstoy card is a set of craft observations for use in revision.
Five scales of place

Think of setting as something that existed before the characters arrived and will continue when they leave. Work at three or more scales. Moving among them lets the reader place a small action within a society and a time.

rows: Try it in a community observatory
A hand reaches from the telescope to the logbook.
Other people nearby and boundaries between them
A workshop light goes off in the room below.
Bicycles are chained to the rail by the entrance.
The old foundry paid for the observatory steps.
The time in history, prices and public news
A change in electricity rates cuts the winter opening hours.

blocks.text: Six jobs a place can do
In “Place in Fiction,” Eudora Welty explores how feeling and belief attach to a particular spot. Decide what practical work each setting is doing in your scene.

rows: Gives the action a physical site
Distance, weather or poverty limits a choice
Reflects a mood; revisit Week 7’s caution about overdoing this
Its habits and history affect events
The sequence of places makes the route of the story
Addresses and prices reveal who belongs where

blocks.text: What things cost

The world includes prices. A character asks about the price of a replacement lens; another counts the coins left in the donation tray. Give an amount and let the two different responses to it reveal their circumstances.
A writer’s card: Faulkner

rows: A recurring county holds families, obligations and burial places across books.
Past events interrupt the present and may feel ongoing.
Voices can alternate; a community may speak as “we.”
Long sentences can connect clauses across generations and moments.

blocks.text: What the present carries

rows: Individual decisions also carry family history.
Grand and plain words may occupy the same line.
Let an earlier use of a place constrain what someone can do there today.

blocks.text: Example: “The cart had to be turned sideways between the pillars the town had erected for a library that had never opened, and the woman who guided it through the gap still had her first library card.” The physical gap makes the old decision relevant to the action.
The joint: the proper noun

Names imply a life for a place outside the present scene. Name what a local would name. Invent a name when an invented place needs one. A name should do more work than a cluster of general adjectives.

rows: Upper Meadow, across the river from the first one

blocks.text: Use real brands sparingly when their main effect would be to date the story. A convincing invented name, like Faulkner’s county or George Eliot’s Middlemarch, can establish local knowledge just as effectively.
Model readings to map

rows: Draw the route from the boy’s door to the bazaar. What do you learn about the street before any person appears?
List the place names. Where does the landscape convey something the girl cannot yet interpret?
A town seen through children’s eyes
Map the route to Nancy’s cabin. Distinguish the physical ditch from what Nancy believes it contains.
List the obstacles in order. How has the path affected the traveler by the end?

blocks.text: Drills, part one

items: 1. Draw a map by hand. Start with a room and a building, then add the street, a transit stop and a place important to another character.
2. Make a price list for ten things in the story.
3. Write a 500-word walk from the narrator’s door to a stop. Consult the street, house and land inventories in Vocabulary.
4. Give the scene weather that changes once.
5. Name ten things a local would name, including a street, a shop and a route.

blocks.text: Drills, continued

items: 6. Use Faulkner’s handling of time as a guide. Write one sentence of about 120 words that holds both a room’s present and its past. Give the writer of the next draft a reason to retain that length.

blocks.text: Pages due

Write roughly 600 words that take the narrator outside once and bring them back again. The trip can be as short as a walk to the street or the next transit stop. Keep the tense of the surrounding story and see what the return lets the narrator notice.
Source notes
Faulkner set many stories in Yoknapatawpha County; Absalom, Absalom! includes a map. Welty’s essay “Place in Fiction” provides a second perspective on the relationship between feeling and location.
Seven ways to be strange
Take an ordinary event from a realist draft. Try handling it in each of the following ways. Cover the first column and identify the kind of story from the bargain it makes with its reader.

rows: Something familiar feels disturbing, though everything could still have happened.
The reader hesitates between a natural and a supernatural explanation.
Henry James, The Turn of the Screw
The extraordinary is part of the world and characters can take it for granted.
Gabriel García Márquez, “A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings”
One impossible premise is pursued with rigorous logic.
One place or thing becomes another without anyone remarking on the change.
Bruno Schulz, The Street of Crocodiles
Buried history returns through a building, family, or landscape.
Edgar Allan Poe, “The Fall of the House of Usher”
Images come together through their imaginative charge across a break in ordinary logic.

blocks.text: Freud’s 1919 essay associates the uncanny with the eeriness of the familiar. Tzvetan Todorov makes hesitation between natural and supernatural explanations central to the fantastic.
Six rules for this exercise

items: 1. Choose one impossibility. Give it room before adding anything else.
2. State it plainly on the first page.
3. Make the surrounding facts exact, down to physical details.
4. Trace consequences through other people, objects, and routines. If a rehearsal room has two Mondays, who gets paid twice?
5. Let the premise stand without explaining its cause.
6. Carry the story through its ending without canceling the events by having the character wake up.

blocks.text: Find the threshold in a realist scene

At a rehearsal, one empty chair faces the wall. Nobody knows who turned it. Everything here is possible. Have the chair return to that angle while the conductor watches it, and the story crosses into a different kind of strangeness. Try locating that threshold in your scene.
The Kafka card

rows: Stay close in third person to someone who never fully understands their predicament.
Use the calm language of an official report.
Give the most unreasonable event a patient, qualified chain of reasoning.
Place individuals in rented spaces, corridors, or offices whose authorities are hard to reach.
Introduce an unexplained impossibility on the first page.
Build a parable or let the search outlast the possible answers.
Follow the impossible first sentence with a calm and practical second one.

blocks.text: Worked example
The committee had abolished Tuesday. The ticket clerk went through the monthly passes with a pencil, starting with the passengers who had paid in advance.
The clerk’s first concern is bookkeeping. Let the practical difficulty carry both the comedy and the unease.
The flat statement

Put the wonder into the event itself. Read a sentence aloud after removing words such as “suddenly,” “strangely,” “somehow,” and “inexplicably.” Listen for the difference between the narrator urging surprise and the fact that earns it. A narrator can also leave an everyday oddity unresolved.

rows: Strangely, the clerk was missing a shadow.
Suddenly the receipts began to sing.
The receipts sang in three parts.
Somehow the bell had learned everyone’s name.
The bell called each passenger by name.

blocks.text: Models to take apart

rows: Underline the opening statement. List the practical things Gregor worries about over the following five pages.
Record who is surprised and who takes events in stride. Examine the final paragraph about telling such a story.
James, The Turn of the Screw (1898)
Make two columns of evidence, one for actual ghosts and one for an ordinary explanation. Compare them at the end.
List everything the story explicitly reveals about what occupies the house. Notice the size of the list.

blocks.text: Six drills

items: 1. Invent five impossible events that could intrude upon one ordinary evening. Give each a single sentence.
2. Choose one event and write ten different opening sentences for it without adverbs.
3. Make a list of ten consequences that would follow if it were true.
4. Rewrite one page so everything feels slightly wrong while every event remains possible.
5. Write 150 words in which one thing becomes another without attracting a comment.
6. Write 150 words using Kafka’s plain announcement and patient chain of consequences.

blocks.text: Pages due
Write about 800 words of your evening with one impossible fact. Keep the tone of the realist draft steady throughout.
Source notes
The uncanny and fantastic distinctions draw on Freud’s “The Uncanny” (1919) and Todorov’s The Fantastic (1970). The seven modes and six working rules are teaching categories used in this course.
The paragraph as a unit of sound
Week 8 examined a sentence on its own. Now listen to what happens as sentences follow each other. The arrangement of pauses, stresses, and lengths gives the paragraph a shape a reader can hear.
Seven paragraph shapes

rows: Each sentence grows longer or stronger.
Several sentences move in one direction until an objection changes it.
Parallel details accumulate without a ranking.
The last sentence answers the first.
One long sentence occupies the paragraph.
Go on for pages without a break.
Hold the reader inside a mind that keeps moving.

blocks.text: Three sources of rhythm

rows: The successive word counts of the sentences.
During this exercise, vary any run of three that sound alike.
The syllables on which your voice lands.
Finish on a beat for closure, or let the voice fall away to leave the thought open.
Vowels and consonants echo across phrases.
Listen for a useful echo and for a cluster that trips your tongue.

blocks.text: Score the pauses
Read a paragraph that uses mostly full stops. Then try the pauses below. A paragraph of full stops can be effective. Hear what alternatives it leaves available.

rows: A held breath between thoughts that lean on each other.
An expectation that the following words fulfill.
A break or change in the voice.

blocks.text: The Woolf card

rows: Let a third-person perspective drift between minds even within a single paragraph.
Admit memories of a lifetime into one day.
Let free indirect thought turn into an image.
Sustain a long sentence with linked clauses and let a parenthesis or a thought interrupt it.
Work in waves of rise, fall, and renewed movement.
Notice light, water, flowers, and the striking hour.
Use a semicolon to hold a connection and an interruption to admit a character’s thought.

blocks.text: Worked example

The orchestra tuned; a note climbed above the others; a string slipped. And the child in the back row (surely someone would begin now?) put both hands flat on the varnished rail to feel the first chord arrive.
Read the three movements of the tuning sentence as one wave. The parenthetical question gives the waiting child a voice within the narration.
The pause mark

Say the following versions aloud. The same events change their relation when only the join changes. The comma splice in the first version is a deliberate rush. Decide what relation you want before choosing the mark.

rows: The soloist nodded, the orchestra began.
The soloist nodded; the orchestra began.
The soloist nodded: the orchestra began.
Offers what follows as the consequence or clarification of what came first.
The soloist nodded — the orchestra began.
The soloist nodded. The orchestra began.

blocks.text: Four models to read aloud

rows: Virginia Woolf, The Waves (1931), first interlude
Mark every semicolon and identify what it joins.
Long, calm sentences keep adding detail.
Count the words in ten consecutive sentences and chart their lengths.
Short sentences and fragments place details separately.
Find passages without a verb and say what each lets you see.
W. G. Sebald, Austerlitz (2001), any ten pages
Long stretches without a paragraph break.
Place possible breaks in the margin. Ask what the unbroken passage gains.

blocks.text: Six drills, all aloud

items: 1. Mark the stressed syllables in a strong paragraph. Read it aloud, move one word, and listen again.
2. Join two facts from your page each of the five ways in the pause-mark table.
3. Rewrite your opening paragraph as a build, a turn, a list, and a single isolated line.
4. Write 300 words of the evening with commas and semicolons, saving the one full stop for the end.
5. Mark all repeated sounds and accidental rhymes on a page. Choose one echo to keep deliberately.
6. Try a 150-word passage with three semicolons and one parenthetical interruption, using Woolf as the formal model.

blocks.text: Pages due
Rescore your story’s three most important paragraphs. Record yourself reading the whole story and mark every stumble in the text.
Source notes

The summary of Woolf’s account of rhythm draws on a 1926 letter and is a paraphrase. The paragraph shapes and punctuation score are course exercises. Check dates in the editions you use when citing the models.
Four ways to build long
As a story grows, several interests compete for attention. Choose a form that gives each line of interest space. These word lengths are rough working guides.

rows: A second strand develops and time can jump substantially.
One sustained line of action can carry the work without a subplot.
Each story stands on its own while a person or place carries across the book.
Chapters can sustain several lines of action across months or years.

blocks.text: Ten architectures

rows: Two stories comment on each other.
A single day contains the book.
A family and its changes over a century.
A tale nested in the occasion of its telling.
William Faulkner, As I Lay Dying
The book repeatedly approaches one event.
Jennifer Egan, A Visit from the Goon Squad
Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

blocks.text: Four parts and their risks

rows: Establish voice, world, and the question.
Change the question at least once.
Stage the few scenes a reader will remember.
Bunching them together weakens their force.
Answer the question in its final form.
Answering an early question the book has already left behind.

blocks.text: Test the middle by naming the question before and after the midpoint. If it stays the same, try a turn that changes what the reader wants to know.
The Flaubert card

rows: Keep an impersonal narrator, without an authorial plea or verdict.
Use free indirect thought so Emma’s imaginings enter the narrator’s grammar.
Use habitual “would” to let the reader feel the repetition of weeks.
Organize three parts around a few widely spaced set pieces.
Place two facts side by side and let the reader make the judgment.
Describe an object closely enough to reveal its owner, then show a repeated action with “would.”

blocks.text: Worked example
The display case had three brass locks and a plywood back fixed with upholstery tacks. Each morning the manager would turn the three keys in order and put the velvet cord across the door.
The difference between the locks and the back does the judging. The repeated locking tells weeks of conduct in one sentence.
Four chapter endings
Think of the chapter as a unit of attention. End it on a change. The gap afterward can carry an entire season, a death, or a change of narrator.

rows: At closing time he handed over the keys.
Leaves a picture with the reader.
A brass key lay sideways in the white plaster dust.
“Then what did you put in the—”

blocks.text: Vary the endings. A hook gains force from the quieter chapters around it.
Four books to chart

rows: Give each chapter one sentence describing its job. Mark the first set piece.
Assign chapters to Anna or Levin and find the first point of contact.
List each return to the central event and record what additional knowledge it brings.
Reduce the action to five sentences. Inventory what the book contains beyond plot.

blocks.text: Seven drills

items: 1. Put your existing evening or short scene inside a whole year. Tell that year in ten sentences.
2. State the premise of the long work in one sentence, then three, then ten.
3. Make fifteen chapter cards. Give each card a want, an obstacle, and a change.
4. Choose one of the ten architectures and explain its fit in a paragraph.
5. Name five set pieces and distribute them among the cards.
6. Write the last line of chapter one three ways, as a hook, a rest, and an image.
7. Write 150 words using Flaubert’s precise object description and one habitual “would” sentence.

blocks.text: Pages due
Submit the fifteen cards and the first two pages of chapter one, about 700 words.
Source notes

Flaubert’s idea of an author present throughout a work yet unseen is paraphrased from an 1852 letter. The word counts are loose conventions and the ten architectures are the course’s working list. Verify editions and dates for formal citations.
Build a system of people
Week 5 built individual characters. In a longer work, one person can reveal a trait, a possibility, or a limit in another. Give every member of the cast an active place in that system.
Eight roles

rows: Possible place in an invented theater story
The stage manager wants the first performance to go ahead.
A competing desire obstructs the protagonist.
An inspector wants the theater closed for repairs.
A contrast brings a particular trait into view.
A meticulous apprentice exposes the manager’s haste.
Conversation lets private thought become speech.
The costumer listens before making a suggestion.
Another life shows a path the protagonist might have taken.
A former colleague has left the stage to teach.
A group speaks as a collective.
The ushers pass on the same rumor.
Someone arrives, changes the situation, and leaves.
A courier delivers a canceled permit.
We know someone through other people, as in week 5.
The missing owner survives in the staff’s incompatible memories.

blocks.text: A nonhuman presence can hold a role too. If a flock breaks into the same call whenever the doors open, its recurrence could serve as a chorus.
Six ways to distinguish people

rows: Can you give each person’s want in five words?
Cover the dialogue tags. Can you tell who speaks?
Name one gesture particular to each person.
Say the names aloud and check for confusable initials or sounds.
Identify what each knows that another person doesn’t.
Find each person’s most revealing opposite.

blocks.text: The triangle

A pair of evenly matched wants can hold a scene in balance. Introduce a third corner—a person, secret, or object—and make someone choose. Consider the stage manager, the inspector, and the only signed permit. Whose interests shift when the permit changes hands?
The Austen card
Austen’s account of a few families in a village suggests a manageable laboratory for contrasts. In Emma, notice how often one person exposes a different aspect of the heroine.

rows: Use an ironic, knowledgeable narrator who remains close to a heroine.
Let free indirect thought involve us in the heroine’s errors.
Let each member of a small community furnish a different foil.
Give each participant a recognizable habit of dialogue.
Assemble the cast for a ball, dinner, or picnic.
Keep clauses balanced and place the sting at the end.
Follow a year, a recognized mistake, and a marriage.
Start with an apparent consensus and gradually disclose whose opinion it is.

blocks.text: Worked example
Everyone at the playhouse understood that the best seat must go to a patron of discernment, and the treasurer had taken the trouble to reserve it for himself.
The sentence borrows the authority of the whole playhouse. Its ending reveals who benefits and whose judgment we have been hearing.
Blocking a group scene
The reader needs a physical map of a room full of speakers. Keep track of who is present, where each person stands, and when a body changes position.

rows: Place everyone in the opening paragraph.
The reader can locate a voice before it speaks.
Give a new speaker an action when the talk changes hands.
The movement identifies the speaker and redirects attention.
Let two speak while the others do things.
The entire group stays present without five simultaneous exchanges.
Use names when pronouns become ambiguous.
A shared pronoun can point to several people in the same room.
Move someone at the turning point.
An entrance, exit, or shift of position marks a change.
The reader sees the gathering from a continuous vantage point.

blocks.text: Worked blocking example

From the prompt desk, the apprentice could see the inspector by the fire door and the treasurer balanced on the stage edge. “Who has the key?” the inspector asked. The treasurer slid off the stage and put both hands in his pockets.
The positions are established before the question. The treasurer answers physically, and the witness can see the movement from the desk.
Four gatherings to study

rows: Jane Austen, Emma (1815), Box Hill picnic
A group turns upon one cruel remark.
List those present and their positions. Mark the sentence that changes the gathering.
A full table filtered through one observer.
Sketch the table and give each guest an identifying act of eating or talking.
Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878), first four chapters
List each person with the single detail that fixes them in mind.
Virginia Woolf, The Waves (1931), first sequence of voices
Give each voice an adjective, then test it against the next thirty pages.

blocks.text: Six drills for the week 18 outline

items: 1. Name eight people in your long work. Give each a role, a want, a gesture, and a speech habit.
2. Build a knowledge table with people down the side and the story’s secrets across the top. Mark who knows what.
3. Form a triangle by adding a third person to an important pair. Write a one-line want for each corner.
4. Say all the names aloud. Replace a pair that rhymes or shares a confusing initial.
5. Remove one character and transfer that person’s job to another character.
6. Try 150 words using Austen’s movement from an apparent general truth toward a particular person’s opinion.

blocks.text: Pages due
Write a scene of about 700 words around a table with five people. Give each a want and keep their locations clear. Include the cast list.
Source notes

Austen’s observation about working with a few families paraphrases an 1814 letter to her niece. The roles, distinguishing tests, and blocking rules are working tools for this course. Check the editions you cite.
Make your own style card

A style emerges from repeated choices about narrator, distance, time, people, place, sentence, and sound. Use the same method you used for nine writers to describe what you actually do. Read a page of your own draft, giving a line of evidence for each choice. Decide which habits to keep and which to test.

rows: What to record from your page
Who speaks, in which person and tense?
Try a close third-person version of a first-person scene.
Where does the narration sit on the distance scale?
Pull back from close interior narration once on a page.
How does thought move or revise itself?
Keep an audible self-correction or trace a different thought pattern.
How much story time passes? Where does memory enter?
Who speaks and who is only recalled?
Give a second person a line of speech.
What sounds, sights, and objects can you recover?
Name three specific things you omitted.
How do statements, fragments, and long sentences alternate?
Try one sustained sentence on a page of short ones.
Where do you use familiar or invented words?
Keep a plain passage and try a single necessary coinage.
How many images recur or extend across the page?
Which two adjectives describe the voice? What earns them?
Retain the tone through a different event.
Do you leave an image, question, answer, or action?
Write a second ending and compare its effect.

blocks.text: Five possible signatures
Find five recurring moves on your own pages. Three deeply characteristic moves can be plenty. Give each one an example, a job, and a risk. The sample lines show the kind of evidence to collect.

rows: “They took the scenery. Even the moon.”
Points to the detail that matters.
Becomes predictable if every paragraph uses it.
Lets a thought change within the sentence.
Names an effect in a particular voice.
Retains the texture of a speaking voice.
A narrator who always shrugs may never discover anything.

blocks.text: Nine writers, nine moves
Collect the nine moves on a single page. Mark the three you used most often.

rows: A small fact beside an understated large feeling.
An object named three times to make an echo.
A body placed exactly in space.
A proper noun and a place with a past.
A flat statement of the impossible.
A semicolon and a parenthetical interruption.
Habitual “would” and an object that judges its owner.
A general truth that contracts into one person’s opinion.

blocks.text: Six constraints

Georges Perec wrote La Disparition (1969) without the letter e. Gilbert Adair preserved that constraint in the English A Void. Invent a temporary rule of your own. Remove it after drafting and see which discoveries survive.

rows: What it forces you to practice
Hear strong beats and short, often Germanic words.
Show the scene through what the narrator observes.
Cap every sentence at ten words
Compress and use the space between sentences.
Fill a page with one sentence
Test how much weight the syntax can carry.

blocks.text: Test a signature
A recognizable gesture earns its place through the work it does in a particular sentence.

rows: Remove it and name exactly what disappears.
Try using it at most once on a page and count the instances.
Change the shape of a second fragment or interruption.
Answer a characteristic fragment with a sustained sentence.
Omit one signature for an entire story and see what takes its place.

blocks.text: Choose three of your five signatures to keep. Write the opposite of each, then use each opposite once in a place where the change will register.
Second capstone • an 8,000-word long story
Build a second strand and a substantial gap in time, as in week 18. Expand a scene you have already written or start a new story.

rows: Establish voice, want, world, and one signature.
Use scenes with another person and an unspoken issue.
Enter another time or place and plant a motif.
Change the governing question and introduce strangeness if the story uses it.
Convey the hardest feeling through observable detail.
Bring the strands together, return the motif changed, and score the final paragraph.

blocks.text: Twelve tests
Run the ten tests from week 10 before adding these final two.

items: 11. Could a reader chart a motif from its first appearance through its transformation?
12. Could a stranger who had read your first story recognize this later story as yours?

blocks.text: After week 20

rows: Transpose a page you wrote yesterday along one craft axis.
Take apart one story from the Map’s reading shelf with a pencil.
Apprentice yourself to another writer. Copy a page by hand, make an author card, and write a short exercise using one observed technique.
Return to the page you began with and write a fresh style card for it.

blocks.text: At this pace a year can yield five finished stories and a dozen author studies. Keep a commonplace book. Copy a sentence by hand, then add one line explaining how it was built. Read living writers as closely as writers from the past. Keep the first page of your own work for the yearly comparison.
Source notes

The constraint example draws on Perec’s La Disparition and Adair’s English translation A Void. The style card is a worksheet for the reader’s own evidence, and the capstone plan, tests, and constraints are course exercises.
